question.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Limit Using the Limit Definition of Euler's Number: Limits Containing Variables
question.worked_solution:
Recall the following special limit: 

$$
e={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}
$$

Now, we rewrite the given limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{nxy} & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{xy} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{xy} \\  & ={e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

judgment.reasoning: q-47077: Both [-2,0] and [-2,1] satisfy the IVT hypotheses. On either interval, f(x)=x+1. Continuity at the right endpoint 1 requires only the left limit, which equals f(1)=2. MA's choice [-2,0] is valid, but its explicit exclusion of [-2,1] is incorrect; the returned choice identifies this additional valid answer. This confirms the earlier source-error judgment. q-118090: Raising (1+1/n)^n to the fixed power xy gives the limit e^{xy}, agreeing with MA. q-118135: Raising (1+x/n)^n to the fixed power y² gives (e^x)^{y²}=e^{xy²}, agreeing with MA.
